Physics: Coverage is broad and well spread across mechanics, electromagnetism, optics, thermal physics and modern physics, with no two items testing essentially the same idea, and every intended key checks out on recomputation (including the multi-step prism, YDSE, mirror and Doppler-with-wind items). The difficulty profile leans easy: a substantial block of one-formula recall questions (q20, q23, q25, q27, q35) sits alongside only a handful of genuinely multi-step items (q7, q9, q15, q26), so adding one or two mid-difficulty computational items would sharpen discrimination. Only small stem-wording fixes are needed; nothing requires rewriting.

[minor] The stem never states that both masses hang freely on either side of a light (massless) pulley, so the intended Atwood arrangement is only implied by the options; add "hang vertically over a light frictionless pulley".

[minor] The phrase "With the same mass attached, the pieces are connected first in series and then in parallel, with their other ends fixed" is muddled about the attachment; state explicitly that in series the pieces are joined end-to-end (one end fixed, mass at the free end) and in parallel both are fixed at one end and jointly carry the mass.
[minor] "with circumradius and radius respectively both 0.12 m" is unidiomatic and forces a re-read; rewrite as "the hexagon's circumradius and the circle's radius are each 0.12 m".

Chemistry: The section covers physical, inorganic and organic chemistry broadly and in roughly the right BITSAT proportions, and every intended key checks out on reworking (including the density-based formula in q57 and the equilibrium combination in q72). Difficulty is mostly appropriate, though a few items (47, 61, 67, 75) are single-line recall while q57 and q59 are the most time-consuming; q59's dense options are still shortcut-able via the diamagnetic Fe(CN)6^4-. The main fixes needed are small wording clarifications (combustion assumption, void occupancy, an inconsistent distractor) and removal of the mild redundancy between the two hydrogen-like-ion numericals.

[minor] The stem never states that combustion is complete to CO2 and H2O, so with the deliberately limiting O2 a student can defend option (A) via incomplete combustion to CO; add "assuming complete combustion" (and drop the irrelevant "after cooling").

[minor] The phrasing "what fraction of its initial concentration remains for X?" is unidiomatic and its antecedent is unclear; rewrite as "at that same instant (both reactions starting together), what fraction of X's initial concentration remains?".

[minor] "A and B occupy, respectively, one-quarter of the tetrahedral and octahedral voids" is ambiguous about whether the one-quarter applies to both void types; state explicitly that A fills one-quarter of the tetrahedral voids and B one-quarter of the octahedral voids (which is what gives the keyed A2BX2).

[minor] Distractor (B) (C2H5ONa then (CH3)3CBr) does not use the stated starting material 2-methylpropan-2-ol at all, so it is inconsistent with the stem; replace it with a sequence that begins from the given alcohol.

[minor] This is essentially the same Bohr-model energy computation for a hydrogen-like ion as q73 (E_n = -13.6Z^2/n^2 applied to a transition); vary one of the two (e.g. make q77 purely about radii/wavelength) to avoid testing the same formula twice.

English Proficiency: The section covers the expected spread of types (error spotting, sentence improvement, synonyms/antonyms, two completion items, two jumbles, idiom, and a two-question RC set), and the passage-based pair plus Q82 and Q86 are well calibrated for the 90-second limit. However, the difficulty is uneven: Q84, Q88, Q90 and Q91 are near-primary-level with distractors that no candidate would pick, which wastes slots that could carry more discriminating vocabulary or grammar work. Tightening the under-constrained jumble in Q87 and raising the floor on the easiest four items would give the section a much more consistent standard.

[major] Because S ("She watered it every morning") is a habitual action with no temporal anchor and R has no linking cue, sequences such as R-P-Q-S (option D) and S-P-R-Q (option B) read just as coherently, so the key A is not uniquely defensible without adding explicit linkers.

[minor] "BRIEF → Short" with wholly unrelated distractors (Distant, Quiet, Careful) is far below BITSAT level and re-tests the same brevity vocabulary already demanded by "laconic" in Q86; replace it with a discriminating synonym item.
[minor] The four options are printed twice (once with a full stop after part D and once without), which must be cleaned up to a single consistent option list before printing.

Logical Reasoning: The section covers a sensible spread of verbal (classification, word formation, syllogism, coding, blood relations), numerical (analogy, series, figure puzzle) and figural (odd figure, mirror image) reasoning, and most items are pitched at the intended easy-to-moderate, 60–90 second level. Two items are unusable as printed: the number analogy admits two defensible keys and the odd-figure item has no figures at all; the syllogism is on the trivial side since conclusion II merely restates a premise. Fix these and the section is print-ready, though a slightly harder series or arrangement item could replace the syllogism to lift the overall difficulty.
[major] Two options are defensible: 36 (digit-sum squared, 2+4=6→36 and 1+5=6→36) and 25 (the n²−1 : (n+1)² pattern, 24=5²−1:36=6² so 15=4²−1:25=5²), so the key C is not unique.
[major] The four option figures are entirely missing (blank options, no figure supplied), so the odd-one-out cannot be attempted or verified against key A.

Mathematics: All forty-five keys check out on independent recomputation, and the topic spread (calculus-heavy with algebra, coordinate geometry, vectors/3-D and probability) matches the BITSAT blueprint with no out-of-syllabus material. The main weakness is difficulty balance: several items (107, 126, 139, 143) are one-step recall that give little discrimination, while only a handful (110, 122, 127, 129, 142) demand real multi-step work within the 90-second budget. Fix the corrupted negation symbols in q131 and the circular phrasing in q114, and swap one of the two line-coplanarity items before printing.
[minor] The stem is circular — "the sum of the first $n$ terms of $\sum_{k=1}^{n}\frac{1}{k(k+2)}" — and should simply read "Evaluate $\sum_{k=1}^{n}\frac{1}{k(k+2)}$".
[major] The negation symbol has been lost in options (A) and (B), which print as "$[eg(p\land q)]\to r$", so the key option (and its distractor) is not a well-formed proposition as typeset.
[minor] Domain of $\sqrt{5-2x}$ is a single-step Class XI recall item, noticeably below BITSAT level; make the function slightly richer (e.g. add a denominator or logarithm).
[minor] This reduces to exactly the same scalar-triple-product coplanarity test for two lines as q119 (there nonzero, here set to zero), so one of the pair should be changed to a different 3-D skill.

Physics: All forty keys check out on reworking (including the multi-step items on prisms, unequal-intensity YDSE, wind-aided Doppler, hexagon–loop field and the two-cell parallel network), and no two items test essentially the same concept. Coverage is well balanced across mechanics, electromagnetism, thermal physics, optics and modern physics, with difficulty pitched at typical BITSAT level; only q2, q7, q19 and q38 push towards the 90-second ceiling but remain reasonable. The four figure-dependent items (2, 8, 28, 33) cannot be validated from text alone and must be checked against the final artwork for consistent labels and values.
[minor] The configuration is under-specified: state explicitly that both masses hang freely from the string over the pulley (Atwood arrangement), since a mass-on-table reading is otherwise possible.

[minor] The clause "with their other ends fixed" only makes sense for the parallel case; rewrite as "first joined end-to-end (series) with the mass at the free end, then both attached between a fixed support and the mass (parallel)".

Chemistry: All forty keys check out numerically and chemically, and the physical/inorganic/organic split (roughly 14/11/11 plus four biomolecule–everyday-life–environment items) is well balanced for BITSAT. The difficulty spread is uneven, though: several one-line recall items (47, 61, 67, 75, 76) sit alongside genuinely demanding ones (57, 59, 72), and five multi-step reagent-sequence questions (52, 58, 60, 71, 78) plus two Bohr-model calculations make the section somewhat repetitive in format. Only small wording fixes and two near-duplicate replacements are needed before printing.

[minor] "The three alkenes below" refers to nothing displayed, since the alkenes appear only inside the options; reword to "the three alkenes listed in the options all hydrogenate to the same alkane".

[minor] "A and B occupy, respectively, one-quarter of the tetrahedral and octahedral voids" is ambiguous about whether the one-quarter applies to both void types; state "one-quarter of the tetrahedral voids and one-quarter of the octahedral voids, respectively" (the intended reading gives A₂BX₂).
[minor] This tests the same VSEPR/hybridisation skill as q51, and XeF₄ itself already appears there as a distractor; replace one of the two with a different p-block property.

[minor] The core computation (hydrogen-like transition energy from E_n = -13.6Z²/n²) duplicates q73; swap one of them for a different atomic-structure concept (e.g. quantum numbers or de Broglie/wavelength).

[minor] "Magnitude of electron gain enthalpy" is ambiguous for Mg, whose Δ_egH is positive (|+230| would exceed Si's 134); phrase it as "increasingly negative electron gain enthalpy" so the intended Si > Na > Al > Mg comparison is unambiguous (key A is unaffected).

English Proficiency: All keys check out and the task mix (error spotting, sentence improvement, synonyms/antonyms, completion, idiom, rearrangement, a two-question RC) matches the BITSAT pattern, with the passage-based pair being well judged. Difficulty is uneven, though: Q82, Q83 and Q86 are demanding while Q84, Q87, Q88, Q90 and Q91 sit at middle-school level, leaving little discrimination in the middle of the range. Dropping the redundant, signposted jumble (87) and upgrading the easiest vocabulary item (88) would even out the section without changing its coverage.

[major] The explicit sequencing markers ("First", "Next", "After that", "A few days later") make the order self-evident, so the item is far too trivial for BITSAT and merely duplicates the rearrangement skill already tested properly in Q85.

[minor] "BRIEF → Short" with three wholly unrelated distractors (Quiet, Distant, Careful) is well below BITSAT vocabulary level and repeats the synonym task of Q83 without adding difficulty; replace the headword with a less elementary one.

[minor] The stem labels the parts (A)–(D) and the options then relabel the same parts differently (the faulty part is (B) in the stem but option D), a conflicting double labelling that invites mismarking.

Logical Reasoning: The section covers a sensible spread of verbal classification, word formation, syllogism, analogy, series, coding, blood relations and figural items, and the difficulty is broadly at BITSAT level with no duplicated skill tested. Keys verified as correct for q96–q100, q102 and q103 (notably the sister/mother direction in q103 and the interleaved +5/−1 and n²−1 patterns in q100). The blocking issue is production-side: q101 has no artwork at all, and the figure-based items (q101, q104, q105) must have their artwork checked against the keys before printing.
[minor] "Which pair is wrongly grouped?" is unidiomatic for an odd-one-out item; replace with "Which pair does not belong to the group?" (the key C is correct).
[minor] The stem's "$\alpha-numeric$" typesets as "α-numeric"; it should read "alphanumeric".
[major] All four options are blank and no figure is attached to the item, so the odd-figure-out question is unanswerable as printed and the key A cannot be checked.

Mathematics: Every intended key in this section checks out on recomputation, and the spread across calculus, algebra, coordinate geometry, vectors/3D and probability matches the BITSAT blueprint well. Difficulty is uneven, though: a cluster of one-step recall items (107, 126, 139, 143) sits next to q127, whose large-number inclusion–exclusion is unsolvable in the time allowed, while q115/q116 repeat the same 5–12–13 harmonic reduction. Rebalancing these few items would give a cleaner, more discriminating 45-question mathematics section.
[minor] The stem is circular/redundant — "the sum of the first $n$ terms of $\sum_{k=1}^{n}\frac{1}{k(k+2)}$" counts the $n$ terms twice; write simply "Evaluate $\sum_{k=1}^{n}\frac{1}{k(k+2)}$".

[minor] This item and q115 both hinge on the identical reduction $5\cos\theta+12\sin\theta=13\cos(\theta-\varphi)$ with the same 5–12–13 triple, so one of the two should be swapped for a different trigonometric skill.

[major] Counting surjections from 10 elements onto 6 requires a six-term inclusion–exclusion with $6^{10},5^{10},4^{10},3^{10}$ and the options differ only in the last two digits, which is far beyond the ~90 s no-calculator budget; use small sets (e.g. 5 onto 3) instead.

[minor] In "A committee of 3 is selected from 8 people, including P and Q", the modifier can attach to the committee (contradicting the question); rephrase as "From 8 people, including P and Q, a committee of 3 is chosen; in how many is at least one of P, Q not selected?".
[minor] Domain of $\sqrt{5-2x}$ is a single-step linear inequality well below BITSAT standard; raise the demand (e.g. $\sqrt{5-2x}$ combined with a logarithm or a denominator) or replace it.
